newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NASDAQ STOCKS FIND EASDAQ MARKET MAKERS SCARCE.
newsitem.headline: NASDAQ STOCKS FIND EASDAQ MARKET MAKERS SCARCE.

text.p: A shortage of market makers knowledgeable on those Nasdaq-quoted companies seeking to list on a new European equivalent, Easdaq, is holding up the number of immediate Easdaq entrants, the European exchange said on Friday.

"Because those companies have been on Nasdaq, few analysts in Europe have been following them and the firms are short of market makers," said Marcel Stappers, managing director of KB-Securities and one of Easdaq's 19 board members.
"I hear there are five or six candidates equipped with market makers, less than initially expected, while there are 70 to 80 European companies now listed on Nasdaq," he added.
Stappers was speaking at a European Venture Capital Association conference in Brussels.
Brussels-based Easdaq - European Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation - will be a quote driven market based on screen trading.

As yet no stocks are listed, though it has been technically operational since September 30. The exchange is modelled on New York's successful Nasdaq market where many European growth companies now seek capital.
To be admitted, firms must be supported by at least two Easdaq-registered market-makers. They must have total assets of 3.5 million Ecus ($4.43 million) and capital and reserves of two million Ecus.

Kredietbank unit KB-Securities lead manages the flotation planned for mid-November of Belgian biotechnology firm Innogenetics - which is 12.5 percent owned by Kredietbank - and that of Belgian-based software firm Artwork Systems.
Stapper said the plan for both was essentially to have a public offering in Belgium, and private placements in other European countries so as to avoid delays.
"The amount of capital raised depends on how much we float," Stapper added. For Innogenetics this could be thirty or forty percent of the company, consisting of both old and new shares.
Two Nasdaq stocks which already have Easdaq market makers are U.S.-based clinical testing firm UniHolding Corp and U.K.-based vehicle management firm Pride Automotive Group .
Canada's Nasdaq-listed bio-tech firm DynaMotive Technologies has also said it plans to seek an Easdaq listing.
Easdaq said its rule book, which has been approved by Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt, is due to be published in Belgium's official gazette in the days ahead.
Belgian newspapers reported this week the rules had already been published in the gazette, but Easdaq said these had in fact been its statutes, not the rules.
It had been initially planned that stocks already quoted on Nasdaq would be listed first so as to build up liquidity for initial public offerings in the following weeks.
Easdaq spokesman Chris Pickles told Reuters on Friday the situation was no cause for concern, adding, "We've never had the feeling we wanted to start with a bang."

The exchange hopes 12 to 15 companies will be trading on Esadaq by the end of the year, building up to 50 in 12 months' time and 500 in five years. Its business plan does not foresee to break even until the fourth year of operations.

Another Easdaq board member, Jos Peeters, said that of the 34 financial institutions that had applied for membership as Easdaq dealers, market makers and/or sponsors, 28 said so far said they wanted to be market makers.
On Easdaq traders will be linked by a computer system modelled on TRAX, the International Securities Markets Association communications system. Deals will be settled by Switzerland's INTERSETTLE.
The Easdaq project originated from contacts between the European Venture Capital Association, European Commission and various market players.
Nasdaq is one of Easdaq's 91 shareholders which brought about 370 million Belgian francs together to finance its launch.
